opus-5.5.text:
Probably the biggest lesson is that the hard part isn't the logic; it's figuring out what the rules actually are. When an organization says "we want our chatbot to answer questions about our HR policy, or our airline refund policy, or our mortgage eligibility rules," they usually assume those rules are written down somewhere, clearly and consistently. When you try to formalize them, translating the natural-language policy into a precise logical model you can reason about, you quickly discover that the document is ambiguous in places and contradictory in others. Sometimes it's silent on cases that matter a lot.

So formalization becomes a kind of mirror. We'll take a policy document, build a logical representation, and run the tools over it. Right away they'll say: "These two clauses can't both be true when an employee is part-time and has been here less than a year." Or: "There's no rule covering this situation at all." Often that's the moment the customer realizes the problem wasn't really the AI. The AI was being asked to be consistent with something that wasn't consistent itself.

The second lesson is that you can't expect domain experts to write logic. Most people who own these policies aren't going to sit down and write formulas in a theorem prover's input language, and they shouldn't have to. So a lot of our work has gone into using the language models themselves to help draft the formal model from the source documents. Then we present that model back in a form people can inspect, question, and refine. It ends up being an iterative conversation between the human, the generative model, and the reasoning engine. The LLM is good at the fuzzy translation. The automated reasoning is good at saying, with mathematical certainty, whether something follows. The human decides what the policy was actually supposed to mean.

Third, once you have that formal model, you can do something really powerful at runtime. When the generative AI produces an answer, you can translate the claims in that answer into the same logical vocabulary and check them. Is this answer actually entailed by the policy? Does it contradict it? Is it just not determined by the rules? That last category is important. Sometimes the right response is "the answer depends on something we don't know yet," and the system can identify which missing fact matters and ask about it. Telling apart "valid," "invalid," and "you need more information" is much more useful than a single confidence score.

The last thing I'd say is that the translation step is where the remaining uncertainty lives, and we have to be honest about that. The reasoning itself is sound, but going from natural language into logic is where errors can creep in. So we've put a lot of effort into techniques like translating multiple ways and checking for agreement, and flagging when the translation itself looks ambiguous. That way the system doesn't overclaim.

The broader takeaway for me is that this is pushing automated reasoning, which historically was used on things like cryptography, hypervisors, and access-control policies, into a world where the "specification" is a human-written document. That turns out to be surprisingly valuable for organizations even apart from the AI. Just getting their rules into a precise, checkable form forces a kind of clarity they've often never had.

r001.rationale: The response says organizations assume their rules are written down, but it does not say those rules are already implicitly formalized in people’s mental models.

r002.rationale: It explains that formalization exposes ambiguous and contradictory policy clauses, including cases where two clauses cannot both be true.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been spending a lot of time on. When you talk to enterprises about what's holding them back from deploying generative AI, hallucination comes up immediately, but when you dig in, the real problem is more specific. They have policies. An airline has rules about when you can rebook a flight. A bank has rules about who's eligible for a certain loan. An HR department has rules about leave. And the question is, when the model says something, is it actually consistent with those rules?

And the interesting thing is that these rules are almost always written down in natural language somewhere, in policy documents, and they're often ambiguous or even contradictory in places that nobody noticed, because a human reading them would just resolve the ambiguity with common sense. So the first thing we learned is that the act of formalizing the rules is itself valuable, independent of the AI. You take the policy document, you translate it into logic, and suddenly you find, oh, these two paragraphs conflict, or this case is just unspecified. That's the same experience we've had for years with formal methods on hardware and distributed systems. The spec is where you find half the bugs.

The second thing is that you don't want to ask the model to do the reasoning. Large language models are quite good at translation, at taking a natural-language statement and mapping it into a formal representation, and they're much less reliable at multi-step logical deduction. So the architecture we landed on is: use the model as a translator, from the policy into logic and from the user's question and the model's answer into logic, and then hand that off to an automated reasoner, an SMT solver or a theorem prover, which actually does the checking. The solver is sound. It doesn't get tired, it doesn't guess. And when it says the answer is valid, it can produce a proof, and when it says it's invalid, it can produce a counterexample, which is incredibly useful because you can hand that back to the model or to a human and say, here's exactly the case where this breaks.

The third lesson is about the translation step, because that's now where the risk lives. If the translation from English to logic is wrong, you can prove something perfectly about the wrong thing. So we've learned to put a lot of effort into making that translation inspectable. You show the user the formalized rules in a way they can read and validate, you generate test scenarios from the logic and ask, does this match your intent, you have the system explain its interpretation in English alongside the formal version. It's a human-in-the-loop process, and it should be. The domain expert is the one who knows what the policy means.

And honestly, the thing that surprised me most is how much this changes the conversation inside organizations. Once the rules are formal, people start arguing about the rules instead of arguing about whether the AI is trustworthy. Which is the right argument to be having.

r001.rationale: The response says people use common sense to resolve ambiguous policy language, but does not state that the rules are already implicitly formalized in people’s mental models.

r002.rationale: It says formalizing policies reveals paragraphs that conflict and cases that are unspecified.

astra-6.text:
One of the things we’ve learned is that the hard part is often figuring out what the rules actually mean. An organization might say, “Only authorized users should have access to this information.” That sounds straightforward, but then you have to ask: Authorized by whom? For which information? Under what circumstances? What happens when two policies disagree?

Formalizing those rules forces that conversation. You uncover ambiguities and assumptions that people may not have realized they were making. And that process is valuable even before you prove anything, because it helps the organization become clearer about what it wants the service to do.

With generative AI, there’s also an important distinction between asking a model to follow a rule and enforcing that rule. You can give the model instructions, but that alone doesn’t establish that every action it takes will comply. If you can express a policy precisely and check a proposed action against it, you have a much stronger basis for deciding whether to allow that action.

But the guarantee is always relative to what you formalized. You still have to ask whether the formal rule captures the organization’s intent. That connection between human intent and a precise specification is really central.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ambiguity in rules and assumptions, but does not say those rules are already implicitly formalized in people’s mental models.

r002.rationale: It mentions asking what happens when policies disagree, but does not state that formalization often reveals inconsistencies in the rules.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing we’ve learned is that figuring out what the rules actually are can be harder than verifying that a system follows them. An organization might have policies written in natural language, but those policies contain ambiguities, exceptions, and assumptions that people resolve without thinking about it. Formalizing them forces you to make those decisions explicit.

With generative AI, that creates an interesting opportunity. You can use a model to help interpret a request or propose an action, and then use formal reasoning to check whether that action satisfies the rules you’ve specified. You don’t have to prove everything about the model to make a useful guarantee about a particular action.

But the guarantee is always relative to the specification. If you’ve written down the wrong rule, a proof won’t fix that. So a lot of the work is getting the people who own the policy involved and making sure that what you’ve formalized really captures what they intend.

r001.rationale: The response says people resolve policy ambiguities and assumptions without thinking, but does not clearly state that the rules are already implicitly formalized in their mental models.

r002.rationale: It mentions ambiguities, exceptions, and assumptions, but does not say that formalization reveals inconsistencies in the rules.
